nameStory: The Slender Spreadwing gets its name from its distinctively thin, delicate body shape and its habit of holding its wings spread out horizontally when at rest, unlike other damselflies that fold their wings back along their bodies. The 'spreadwing' part comes from this unique wing position, making them easy to spot among the cattails and pond vegetation where they perch.
description: The Slender Spreadwing is a delicate damselfly with an extra-thin body that looks almost thread-like compared to other damselflies. Its body is primarily black with a striking pale blue face that stands out like a tiny mask. The wings have distinctive yellow edges that catch the light, with females showing more pronounced pale yellow coloring on their wings and growing noticeably larger than males.

idTips.label: Wings held horizontally
idTips.description: Unlike most damselflies that fold wings along their body, spreadwings hold their wings out to the sides when perched, creating a distinctive T-shape silhouette

idTips.label: Pale blue face
idTips.description: The face has a distinctive pale blue coloring that contrasts sharply with the black body, looking like a tiny blue mask when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Yellow wing edges
idTips.description: Wings have yellow coloring along the edges that creates a subtle golden outline, more pronounced in females and visible when backlit by sunlight

idTips.label: Extra-thin body
idTips.description: The body appears unusually slender even for a damselfly, giving it an almost needle-like appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Black body coloration
idTips.description: The thorax and abdomen are predominantly black with metallic sheen that may show hints of green or bronze in bright sunlight

habitat: Look for Slender Spreadwings around springs, small ponds, and seasonal pools that may dry up later in the year. They prefer areas with emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and rushes where they can perch horizontally on stems. These damselflies are often found in slightly cooler, shaded areas near water sources with good water quality.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but are not yet at peak numbers. Look for freshly emerged individuals with softer coloration near breeding waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and actively mating. Best time for identification as colors are brightest and behavior is most observable around ponds and springs.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, though numbers decline. Late-season individuals may show more worn wing edges and slightly faded coloration.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they overwinter as eggs laid in plant stems near water, waiting for spring warmth to trigger development.

funFact: Female Slender Spreadwings use their saw-like egg-laying organ to slice neat rows of cuts into plant stems, depositing eggs that will survive being completely frozen solid through New England winters and still hatch perfectly healthy the following spring.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spreadwings, but the Slender Spreadwing lives up to its name with the thinnest body in the group. Remember: 'Slender means thinner' - if the body looks extra-thin even for a spreadwing, and has that pale blue face, you've found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'damselfly' comes from their delicate appearance compared to the more robust dragonflies, but don't let the dainty name fool you - they're skilled predators with excellent eyesight. Spreadwings belong to an ancient family that holds their wings differently from most other damselflies.
compareHints: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration. The Emerald Spreadwing has a green metallic sheen and broader body, while the Spotted Spreadwing shows distinct markings on the wings. The amber-winged species have obviously amber-tinted wings rather than the subtle yellow edges of the Slender Spreadwing.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots.
Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle.
Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
